\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We measure a lower bound on the generational depth discrimination boundary $\Kempirical$ for prompt-chain recursive synthetic text.
$\Kempirical \leq 3$ across all ten configurations (six architecture families, 1B--8B) at $\theta{=}0.60$; for general web text, $\Kempirical \leq 2$ regardless of model family or scale, while structured academic text (arXiv) reaches $\Kempirical{=}3$ across two independent architectures.
Among the six nominal $\Kempirical{=}2$ web text configurations, four retain significance under Bonferroni correction; the two marginal cases reflect narrow effect sizes rather than classification failure.
This one-wash laundering effect means that a single generation pass renders web text statistically indistinguishable from deeper recursive content, concentrating all exploitable signal at the 0v1 boundary.

The practical consequence is direct: for web text, binary filtering (depth 0 vs.\ $\geq$1) captures the only reliable discrimination signal, and graduated weighting beyond $\Kempirical$ injects noise from near-random depth assignments.
The consistency check confirms this prediction, with binary curation most effectively minimizing MMLU degradation among six strategies tested ($-$0.77\,pp vs.\ $-$1.53\,pp for no-filter; Section~\ref{sec:filtering}).
For structured domains where $\Kempirical{=}3$, graduated strategies can exploit one additional depth level, so corpus curators should calibrate their filtering approach to the source domain rather than assuming a universal boundary.

The 15 statistical features enable deployment across generators without retraining: continuation-mode classifiers retain 80--92\% accuracy across model families, and feature rankings remain stable ($\rho > 0.90$) under alternative scorers.
This scorer independence makes the framework applicable to corpora generated by unknown or heterogeneous models, the common scenario in web-scale data curation where the generating model is rarely identified.
$\Kempirical$ converts a continuous AUC decay surface into a discrete operating boundary, providing a principled basis for curation design that replaces ad hoc depth thresholds with a measurement grounded in the Data Processing Inequality.

Several directions remain open.
As model scale increases, the 0v1 signal attenuates (JSD $0.077$ at 8B vs.\ $0.15$--$0.27$ at $\leq$1.5B), suggesting that models beyond 13B may increasingly yield $\Kempirical{=}1$, collapsing depth estimation to the binary boundary already dominant at current scales; tracking this trend is important for the continued viability of depth estimation.
$\Kempirical$ is feature-set dependent: the 15D features provide a conservative lower bound, while neural probes extend it by one level for some architectures but sacrifice cross-model consistency.
The retrain-chain setting, where each generation also modifies model parameters, yields substantially higher $\Kempirical$ ($\geq$4 for Pythia-1.4B LoRA); bridging the prompt-chain and retrain-chain boundaries would connect our text-level measurement to the model collapse literature.
Extending the measurement to models beyond 8B, additional structured domains (legal, medical text, where stylistic constraints may amplify depth signal as observed for arXiv), and scorer-ensemble strategies for improved robustness at marginal boundaries are natural next steps.
As recursive synthetic content continues to accumulate in web corpora, $\Kempirical$ offers a quantitative basis for deciding how much depth resolution a curation pipeline can extract, anchoring filtering decisions in measurement rather than assumption.
